title: Oracle SQL Reviewer Question Bank 201-249 (Corrected v2)
description: Corrected bank with exact reviewer sequence, separated tables, readable SQL, detailed explanations, and neutral technical clarifications.

questions.stem: Which three SQL statements display the value 1890.55 as $1,890.55?

sections.title: Required output
sections.content:
$1,890.55
The format must include a dollar sign, a thousands separator, and exactly two decimal places.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(1890.55, '$9G999D00') FROM dual;
options.explanation: $ displays the currency symbol, G displays the group separator, and D00 displays the decimal separator followed by two digits.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(1890.55, '$9,999V99') FROM dual;
options.explanation: V scales the number rather than displaying a decimal separator, so it does not produce the required currency format.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(1890.55, '$00G000D00') FROM dual;
options.explanation: The format includes a currency symbol, group separator, decimal separator, and two required decimal digits.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(1890.55, '$99,999D99') FROM dual;
options.explanation: This format includes extra leading digit positions and uses mixed literal and NLS-sensitive separators, so it is not one of the document’s marked answers.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(1890.55, '$9G999D99') FROM dual;
options.explanation: G and D use the applicable NLS group and decimal characters, while 99 displays the two decimal digits.

questions.answerExplanation: $ displays the currency symbol, G displays the group separator, and D00 displays the decimal separator followed by two digits. The format includes a currency symbol, group separator, decimal separator, and two required decimal digits. G and D use the applicable NLS group and decimal characters, while 99 displays the two decimal digits.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about self-joins?

options.text: They require the EXISTS operator in the join condition.
options.explanation: A self-join normally relates two aliases of the same table using a standard join condition. EXISTS is not required.

options.text: They have no join condition.
options.explanation: A meaningful self-join normally has a condition that relates rows from the two references to the same table.

options.text: They require the NOT EXISTS operator in the join condition.
options.explanation: NOT EXISTS is not a requirement for a self-join.

options.text: They require table aliases.
options.explanation: Separate aliases distinguish the two references to the same table and allow their columns to be qualified.

options.text: They are always equijoins.
options.explanation: A self-join can use equality, inequality, range, inner-join, or outer-join conditions.

options.text: They can use INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN.
options.explanation: A self-join may be implemented using inner-join or outer-join syntax, depending on the required result.

questions.answerExplanation: Separate aliases distinguish the two references to the same table and allow their columns to be qualified. A self-join may be implemented using inner-join or outer-join syntax, depending on the required result.

questions.stem: A subquery is called a single-row subquery when ________.

options.text: There is only one subquery in the outer query and the inner query returns one or more values.
options.explanation: The number of subqueries in the outer query does not determine whether a subquery is a single-row subquery.

options.text: The inner query returns a single value to the outer query.
options.explanation: A single-row subquery returns no more than one row to the parent statement and is commonly used with single-row comparison operators.

options.text: The inner query uses an aggregating function and returns one or more values.
options.explanation: An aggregate function may return one value, but using an aggregate function is not the defining requirement.

options.text: The inner query returns one or more values and the outer query returns a single value.
options.explanation: The outer query’s result size does not define the inner query as a single-row subquery.

questions.answerExplanation: A single-row subquery returns no more than one row to the parent statement and is commonly used with single-row comparison operators.

questions.stem: You must write a query that prompts for column names and conditions every time it is executed. The user must be prompted only once for the table name. Which statement achieves these objectives?

sections.title: Requirement
sections.content:
Prompt every execution for both column names and the condition.
A single & is used for repeated prompting, while && defines and retains the table-name substitution variable.
Prompt only once for the table name and retain that value.

options.text: SELECT &col1, &col2 FROM &table WHERE &condition = '&cond';
options.explanation: The table variable uses a single &, so it is not automatically retained for later execution.

options.text: SELECT &col1, &col2 FROM '&table' WHERE &condition = &cond;
options.explanation: Single quotation marks turn the table substitution into character text rather than a valid table identifier.

options.text: SELECT &col1, &col2 FROM &&table WHERE &condition = '&cond';
options.explanation: &col1, &col2, &condition, and &cond prompt when undefined. &&table prompts once and defines the table variable for reuse.

options.text: SELECT &col1, &col2 FROM &&table WHERE &condition = &&cond;
options.explanation: &&cond retains the condition value, but the requirement says that the condition value should be prompted every time.

questions.answerExplanation: &col1, &col2, &condition, and &cond prompt when undefined. &&table prompts once and defines the table variable for reuse.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true regarding single-row functions?

options.text: The data type returned can be different from the data type of the referenced argument.
options.explanation: Conversion functions can accept one data type and return another, such as TO_CHAR converting a number or date to character data.

options.text: They can return multiple values for more than one data type.
options.explanation: A single-row function returns one result for each input row.

options.text: They can accept only one argument.
options.explanation: Some functions accept one argument, while others accept two or more.

options.text: They can be nested only to two levels.
options.explanation: Single-row functions can be nested beyond two levels when the returned data types remain compatible.

options.text: They can be used in SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY clauses.
options.explanation: Single-row functions can calculate displayed values, filter rows, and provide sort expressions.

options.text: They can accept column names, expressions, variable names, or user-supplied constants as arguments.
options.explanation: Function arguments may include columns, literals, variables, and valid expressions.

questions.answerExplanation: Conversion functions can accept one data type and return another, such as TO_CHAR converting a number or date to character data. Single-row functions can calculate displayed values, filter rows, and provide sort expressions. Function arguments may include columns, literals, variables, and valid expressions.

questions.stem: Examine the DEPARTMENTS table and the compound query. Which two ORDER BY clauses can be used to sort the output?

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT dep_name, 'b'
FROM departments
WHERE department_id = 90
UNION
SELECT department_id, department_name DEPT_NAME, 'a'
FROM departments
WHERE department_id = 10;

options.text: ORDER BY DEPT_NAME;
options.explanation: A compound query can sort by a result-column name or alias established by the first SELECT. In the displayed text, DEPT_NAME is not consistently exposed as the first result-column alias, so this is not selected.

options.text: ORDER BY DEPT_ID;
options.explanation: The reviewer treats DEPT_ID as a valid result-column alias from the first SELECT. A final ORDER BY may refer to that alias after the complete compound query.

options.text: ORDER BY 'b';
options.explanation: ORDER BY 'b' sorts by the constant literal b. Every row has the same sort key, so it does not meaningfully order the compound result by an output column.

options.text: ORDER BY 3;
options.explanation: ORDER BY 3 refers to the third output column by position. Positional ordering is valid in the single ORDER BY placed after the complete compound query.

questions.answerExplanation: The reviewer treats DEPT_ID as a valid result-column alias from the first SELECT. A final ORDER BY may refer to that alias after the complete compound query. ORDER BY 3 refers to the third output column by position. Positional ordering is valid in the single ORDER BY placed after the complete compound query.
questions.technicalNote: The visible compound query has an inconsistent select-list transcription: the first SELECT appears to show fewer columns than the second, while the answer key refers to DEPT_ID and column position 3. The reviewer scoring B and D is preserved using the intended three-column compound result.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about the WHERE and HAVING clauses in a SELECT statement?

options.text: The WHERE and HAVING clauses can be used in the same statement only if they are applied to different columns.
options.explanation: The clauses can reference the same column when appropriate. Their distinction is based on when filtering occurs.

options.text: Aggregate functions and columns used in HAVING must be specified in the query’s SELECT list.
options.explanation: An aggregate expression can be used in HAVING without being displayed in the select list.

options.text: The WHERE clause can exclude rows after dividing them into groups.
options.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.

options.text: The HAVING clause can be used with aggregate functions in subqueries.
options.explanation: A subquery may group rows and use HAVING to filter its aggregate results.

options.text: The WHERE clause can exclude rows before dividing them into groups.
options.explanation: Rows rejected by WHERE do not participate in the later grouping and aggregate calculations.

questions.answerExplanation: A subquery may group rows and use HAVING to filter its aggregate results. Rows rejected by WHERE do not participate in the later grouping and aggregate calculations.

questions.stem: You must create an EMPLOYEES table. EMPLOYEE_ID, EMPLOYEE_NAME, LOYEES_ID, and LOGIN_ID must be unique and not null. Which two statements create the required table?

sections.title: Requirements
items: The specified identifier and login columns must reject nulls and duplicate values.

options.text: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id NUMBER, login_id NUMBER, employee_name VARCHAR2(100), hire_date DATE, CONSTRAINT emp_id_uk UNIQUE (employee_id, login_id));
options.explanation: A composite unique constraint permits multiple rows containing null components and does not individually make both columns non-null.

options.text: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id NUMBER, login_id NUMBER, employee_name VARCHAR2(25), hire_date DATE, CONSTRAINT emp_id_pk PRIMARY KEY (employee_id, login_id));
options.explanation: A composite primary key makes both key columns unique as a combination and implicitly NOT NULL.

options.text: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id NUMBER CONSTRAINT emp_id_pk PRIMARY KEY, login_id NUMBER UNIQUE, employee_name VARCHAR2(25), hire_date DATE);
options.explanation: The unique constraint on LOGIN_ID permits nulls unless NOT NULL is also declared.

options.text: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id NUMBER, login_id NUMBER, employee_name VARCHAR2(100), hire_date DATE, CONSTRAINT emp_id_uk UNIQUE (employee_id, login_id), CONSTRAINT emp_id_nn NOT NULL (employee_id, login_id));
options.explanation: A NOT NULL constraint cannot be declared as a table-level constraint over multiple columns using this syntax.

options.text: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id NUMBER CONSTRAINT emp_id_nn NOT NULL, login_id NUMBER CONSTRAINT login_id_nn NOT NULL, employee_name VARCHAR2(100), hire_date DATE, CONSTRAINT emp_num_id_uk UNIQUE (employee_id, login_id));
options.explanation: Both columns are explicitly NOT NULL, and the composite UNIQUE constraint prevents duplicate employee-and-login combinations.

questions.answerExplanation: A composite primary key makes both key columns unique as a combination and implicitly NOT NULL. Both columns are explicitly NOT NULL, and the composite UNIQUE constraint prevents duplicate employee-and-login combinations.

questions.stem: In your session, NLS_DATE_FORMAT is set to DD-MON-RR. Which two queries display the year as four digits?

sections.title: Session setting
sections.content:
NLS_DATE_FORMAT = 'DD-MON-RR'
The session’s default display uses a two-digit RR year unless an explicit four-digit format is applied.

options.text: SELECT TO_DATE(SYSDATE, 'RRRR-MM-DD') FROM dual;
options.explanation: SYSDATE is already a date. TO_DATE does not format a date for display and introduces an unnecessary implicit conversion.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'MM/DD/YYYY') FROM dual;
options.explanation: YYYY explicitly formats the year using four digits.

options.text: SELECT TO_DATE(ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, 6), 'dd-mon-yyyy') FROM dual;
options.explanation: ADD_MONTHS already returns a date, and TO_DATE is not the correct function for formatting it for display.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, 6)) FROM dual;
options.explanation: Without an explicit format model, the conversion uses the session’s DD-MON-RR setting and displays a two-digit year.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, 6), 'dd-mon-yyyy') FROM dual;
options.explanation: The explicit YYYY format element displays the year as four digits.

options.text: SELECT TO_DATE(TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'MM/DD/YYYY'), 'MM/DD/YYYY') FROM dual;
options.explanation: The final result is a DATE, whose display again follows NLS_DATE_FORMAT, which uses a two-digit year.

questions.answerExplanation: YYYY explicitly formats the year using four digits. The explicit YYYY format element displays the year as four digits.

questions.stem:
Examine the types and examples of relationship that follow:

1 One-to-one
2 One-to-many
3 Many-to-one
4 Many-to-many

a) Teacher to Student
b) Employees to Manager
c) Person to SSN
d) Customers to Products

Which option indicates correctly matched relationships?

options.explanation: This assigns Customers to Products to one-to-one and Teacher to Student to many-to-one, which does not match the reviewer’s intended mapping.
This maps Person to SSN as one-to-one and Customers to Products as one-to-many, differing from the source mapping.
This is a natural literal pairing of each numbered relationship with the example written on the same source line, but it is not the option highlighted by the reviewer.

This is the matching sequence highlighted in the reviewer: Person-to-SSN for one-to-one, Teacher-to-Student for one-to-many, Employees-to-Manager for many-to-one, and Customers-to-Products for many-to-many.

questions.answerExplanation: This is the matching sequence highlighted in the reviewer: Person-to-SSN for one-to-one, Teacher-to-Student for one-to-many, Employees-to-Manager for many-to-one, and Customers-to-Products for many-to-many.
questions.technicalNote: This is a matching-type question. The source places example letters beside relationship lines, which can suggest a different literal pairing. The official highlighted mapping is D and remains the scoring key.

questions.stem: A non-correlated subquery can be defined as __________.

options.text: A set of sequential queries in which the result of the inner query is used as the search value in the outer query.
options.explanation: A non-correlated subquery executes independently, and its result is supplied to the outer query.

options.text: A set of sequential queries, all of which must return values from the same table.
options.explanation: The subquery and outer query may retrieve data from different tables.

options.text: A set of sequential queries, all of which must always return a single value.
options.explanation: A non-correlated subquery may return one row, multiple rows, or no rows, depending on how it is used.

options.text: A SELECT statement that can be embedded only in a clause of another SELECT statement.
options.explanation: Subqueries may also be used in DML and other supported SQL statements.

questions.answerExplanation: A non-correlated subquery executes independently, and its result is supplied to the outer query.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about the USING clause when joining tables?

options.text: It is used to specify an equijoin of columns that have the same name in both tables.
options.explanation: USING(column_name) creates an equality comparison between columns that have the same name in both joined row sources. The shared column is returned once in the joined result.

options.text: It is used to specify an explicit join condition involving operators.
options.explanation: ON is used for arbitrary join conditions, including differently named columns, non-equality operators, or multiple expressions. USING is limited to same-named equijoin columns.

options.text: It can never be used with natural joins.
options.explanation: NATURAL JOIN automatically chooses all same-named compatible columns, so a separate USING clause is not written with the same join specification.

options.text: It can never be used with a full outer join.
options.explanation: A FULL OUTER JOIN can use USING when both tables contain the same-named join column.

options.text: All column names in a USING clause must be qualified with a table name or table alias.
options.explanation: The reviewer selects this statement, but columns inside USING are normally written unqualified, for example USING (department_id), not table_alias.department_id.

questions.answerExplanation: USING(column_name) creates an equality comparison between columns that have the same name in both joined row sources. The shared column is returned once in the joined result. The reviewer selects this statement, but columns inside USING are normally written unqualified, for example USING (department_id), not table_alias.department_id.
questions.technicalNote: The reviewer selects A and E. In Oracle syntax, a column named inside USING is normally unqualified. The practical rule is that USING identifies same-named equijoin columns, while ON handles explicitly qualified or more complex conditions.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true regarding subqueries?

options.text: A main query can have many subqueries.
options.explanation: One parent statement can contain multiple subqueries in supported clauses and expressions.

options.text: A subquery can have more than one main query.
options.explanation: A subquery belongs to its containing parent query or statement.

options.text: The subquery and main query must retrieve data from the same table.
options.explanation: The inner and outer queries may retrieve data from different tables.

options.text: The subquery and main query can retrieve data from different tables.
options.explanation: The tables referenced by the inner and outer queries do not have to be the same.

options.text: Only one column or expression can be compared between the subquery and main query.
options.explanation: Oracle supports multiple-column subqueries and row-value comparisons.

options.text: Multiple columns or expressions can be compared between the subquery and main query.
options.explanation: Compatible combinations of columns or expressions may be compared between the query blocks.

questions.answerExplanation: One parent statement can contain multiple subqueries in supported clauses and expressions. The tables referenced by the inner and outer queries do not have to be the same. Compatible combinations of columns or expressions may be compared between the query blocks.

questions.stem: Examine the PROMOTIONS table and the SQL statement. What is the outcome?

sections.title: Requirement
sections.content: Find the average promotion cost for category A in the ranges $0–2000 and $2001–5000.

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT AVG(CASE
WHEN promo_cost BETWEEN 0 AND 2000
AND promo_category = 'A'
THEN promo_cost
ELSE NULL
END) "CAT_2000A",
AVG(CASE
WHEN promo_cost BETWEEN 2001 AND 5000
AND promo_category = 'A'
THEN promo_cost
ELSE NULL
END) "CAT_5000A"
FROM promotions;

options.text: It generates an error because multiple conditions cannot be specified for the WHEN clause.
options.explanation: Multiple conditions can be combined with AND in a searched CASE expression.

options.text: It executes successfully and gives the required result.
options.explanation: Each CASE returns PROMO_COST for its specified range and category. AVG ignores the null results and calculates each conditional average.

options.text: It generates an error because CASE cannot be used with group functions.
options.explanation: A CASE expression can be used as the argument of an aggregate function.

options.text: It generates an error because NULL cannot be specified as a return value.
options.explanation: A CASE expression may return null, and AVG ignores null values.

questions.answerExplanation: Each CASE returns PROMO_COST for its specified range and category. AVG ignores the null results and calculates each conditional average.

questions.stem: Examine the ORDER_ITEMS table. Which two queries return rows where QUANTITY is a multiple of ten?

options.text: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE quantity = TRUNC(quantity, -1);
options.explanation: TRUNC(quantity,-1) removes the units digit. Equality holds when the original quantity already ends in zero, so this expression is a direct test for multiples of ten.

options.text: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE quantity / 10 = TRUNC(quantity);
options.explanation: For quantity 20, quantity/10 is 2 while TRUNC(quantity) is 20. The comparison uses different scales and does not test divisibility by ten.

options.text: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE FLOOR(quantity / 10) = TRUNC(quantity);
options.explanation: The reviewer highlights this expression, but FLOOR(quantity/10) is roughly one tenth of quantity and is not equal to TRUNC(quantity) for ordinary positive multiples such as 20.

options.text: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE quantity = ROUND(quantity, 1);
options.explanation: QUANTITY is an integer column. ROUND(quantity,1) leaves every integer unchanged, so this condition includes values that are not multiples of ten.

options.text: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE MOD(quantity, 10) = 0;
options.explanation: MOD(quantity,10) returns the remainder after division by ten. A remainder of zero means the quantity is a multiple of ten.

questions.answerExplanation: The reviewer highlights this expression, but FLOOR(quantity/10) is roughly one tenth of quantity and is not equal to TRUNC(quantity) for ordinary positive multiples such as 20. MOD(quantity,10) returns the remainder after division by ten. A remainder of zero means the quantity is a multiple of ten.
questions.technicalNote: The reviewer selects C and E. A also directly identifies integer values ending in zero, while C does not evaluate as a divisibility test for ordinary positive quantities. Scoring remains C and E, with this clarification shown after submission.

questions.stem: Examine the query below, which executes successfully. What is the result?

codeBlocks.title: Query

options.text: It returns rows that are not common to both SELECT statements.
options.explanation: This describes a difference operation, not UNION ALL.

options.text: It returns rows from both SELECT statements after eliminating duplicate rows.
options.explanation: UNION removes duplicate rows, while UNION ALL retains them.

options.text: It returns rows common to both SELECT statements.
options.explanation: This describes INTERSECT.

options.text: It returns rows from both SELECT statements, including duplicate rows.
options.explanation: UNION ALL combines all rows without performing duplicate elimination.

questions.answerExplanation: UNION ALL combines all rows without performing duplicate elimination.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true regarding multiple-row subqueries?

options.text: They can contain group functions.
options.explanation: A multiple-row subquery can use aggregate functions, often together with grouping, to return multiple aggregate results.

options.text: They always contain a subquery within a subquery.
options.explanation: A multiple-row subquery does not require another nested subquery.

options.text: They use the < ALL operator to imply less than the maximum.
options.explanation: < ALL means less than every returned value, which normally means less than the minimum returned value.

options.text: They can be used to retrieve multiple rows from a single table only.
options.explanation: Multiple-row subqueries may retrieve data from joins, views, or other supported row sources.

options.text: They should not be used with the NOT IN operator in the main query if NULL is likely to be part of the subquery result.
options.explanation: If the subquery result contains null, a NOT IN comparison can evaluate to unknown and return no rows unexpectedly.

questions.answerExplanation: A multiple-row subquery can use aggregate functions, often together with grouping, to return multiple aggregate results. If the subquery result contains null, a NOT IN comparison can evaluate to unknown and return no rows unexpectedly.

questions.stem:
View the Exhibit and examine the structure of the CUSTOMERS and CUST_HISTORY tables.

The CUSTOMERS table contains only active customers.

The CUST_HISTORY table stores historical details relating to changes in the location of current customers as well as previous customers who are no longer active with the company.

You need to find customers who have never changed their address.

Which SET operator would you use to get the required output?

options.text: INTERSECT
options.explanation: INTERSECT returns rows appearing in both query results.

options.text: UNION ALL
options.explanation: UNION ALL combines both result sets and keeps duplicate rows.

options.text: MINUS
options.explanation: MINUS returns rows from the first result that are not present in the second result.

options.text: UNION
options.explanation: UNION combines both results and removes duplicates rather than subtracting historical customers.

questions.answerExplanation: MINUS returns rows from the first result that are not present in the second result.
questions.technicalNote: MINUS should compare compatible customer identifiers or matching customer columns from the current-customer query against the history query. The two complete tables have different structures, so SELECT * cannot be used directly for this set operation.

questions.stem:
View the Exhibit and examine the PRODUCTS and ORDER_ITEMS tables.

You executed the following query to display PRODUCT_NAME and the number of times the product has been ordered:

What would happen when the above statement is executed?

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT p.product_name, i.item_cnt
FROM (
  SELECT product_id, COUNT(*) item_cnt
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY product_id
) i RIGHT OUTER JOIN products p
  ON i.product_id = p.product_id;

options.text: The statement executes successfully and produces the required output.
options.explanation: Inline views can be used with outer joins, the alias ITEM_CNT is available to the outer query, and grouping is allowed inside the inline view.

options.text: The statement does not execute because inline views and outer joins cannot be used together.
options.explanation: An inline view can participate in an outer join.

options.text: The statement does not execute because the ITEM_CNT alias cannot be displayed in the outer query.
options.explanation: An inline-view column alias can be referenced by the outer query.

options.text: The statement does not execute because GROUP BY cannot be used in the inline view.
options.explanation: An inline view may contain GROUP BY and aggregate functions.

questions.answerExplanation: Inline views can be used with outer joins, the alias ITEM_CNT is available to the outer query, and grouping is allowed inside the inline view.
questions.technicalNote: The expected output was removed from the question body. The RIGHT OUTER JOIN preserves every product; products with no matching order-item group receive NULL for ITEM_CNT. This derivation appears only after submission.

questions.stem: Which statement is true regarding the UNION operator?

options.text: By default, the output is not sorted.
options.explanation: This statement is not highlighted as correct in the document.

options.text: Null values are not ignored during duplicate checking.
options.explanation: Corresponding null values participate when UNION compares complete rows and eliminates duplicates.

options.text: The names of all columns must be identical across all SELECT statements.
options.explanation: Corresponding columns need compatible data types, but their names do not have to be identical.

options.text: The number of columns selected in all SELECT statements need not be the same.
options.explanation: Each component query must return the same number of columns.

questions.answerExplanation: Corresponding null values participate when UNION compares complete rows and eliminates duplicates.

questions.stem: You issued the following command: DROP TABLE employees; Which three statements are true?

options.text: All uncommitted transactions are committed.
options.explanation: DROP TABLE is a DDL statement, so Oracle implicitly commits the current transaction.

options.text: All indexes and constraints defined on the table being dropped are also dropped.
options.explanation: The indexes and constraints belonging to the table are removed with the table.

options.text: Sequences used in the EMPLOYEES table become invalid.
options.explanation: Sequences are independent schema objects and remain valid after the table is dropped.

options.text: The space used by the EMPLOYEES table is reclaimed immediately.
options.explanation: Without PURGE, an eligible table may be retained in the recycle bin.

options.text: The EMPLOYEES table can be recovered using the ROLLBACK command.
options.explanation: DROP TABLE cannot be reversed using ROLLBACK. An eligible table may instead be recovered using Flashback Drop.

options.text: The EMPLOYEES table is moved to the recycle bin.
options.explanation: Without PURGE, an eligible dropped table is moved to the recycle bin.

questions.answerExplanation: DROP TABLE is a DDL statement, so Oracle implicitly commits the current transaction. The indexes and constraints belonging to the table are removed with the table. Without PURGE, an eligible dropped table is moved to the recycle bin.

questions.stem:
Examine the CREATE TABLE statements for the STORES and SALES tables.

You execute the following statement.

The statement fails due to the integrity constraint error.

Which three options ensure that the statement will execute successfully?

codeBlocks.title: STORES table
SALES table
codeBlocks.code:
CREATE TABLE sales (
  sales_id NUMBER(4) CONSTRAINT sales_id_pk PRIMARY KEY,
  item_id NUMBER(4),
  quantity NUMBER(10),
  sales_date DATE,
  store_id NUMBER(4),
  CONSTRAINT store_id_fk FOREIGN KEY (store_id)
    REFERENCES stores(store_id)
);

codeBlocks.title: DELETE statement
codeBlocks.code:
DELETE FROM stores
WHERE store_id = 900;

codeBlocks.title: Error
codeBlocks.code: ORA-02292: integrity constraint (HR.STORE_ID_FK) violated

options.text: Disable the primary key in the STORES table.
options.explanation: Disabling the parent primary key does not remove the child SALES rows that reference STORE_ID 900. The dependent relationship remains the reason the parent row cannot be deleted safely.

options.text: Use the CASCADE keyword with the DELETE statement.
options.explanation: Oracle DELETE syntax does not accept a general CASCADE keyword. Cascading deletion must be defined on the foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE.

options.text: Delete the rows with STORE_ID = 900 from the SALES table and then delete the row from the STORES table.
options.explanation: Deleting the dependent SALES rows first removes the foreign-key references. The STORES row can then be deleted without violating referential integrity.

options.text: Disable the foreign key in the SALES table and then delete the row.
options.explanation: Disabling STORE_ID_FK stops Oracle from checking the relationship during the delete, allowing the parent row to be removed. This can leave orphaned child rows and requires controlled use.

options.text: Create the foreign key in the SALES table on SALES_ID with the ON DELETE CASCADE option.
options.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE on the child foreign key makes Oracle delete matching SALES rows automatically when the referenced STORES row is deleted.

questions.answerExplanation: Deleting the dependent SALES rows first removes the foreign-key references. The STORES row can then be deleted without violating referential integrity. Disabling STORE_ID_FK stops Oracle from checking the relationship during the delete, allowing the parent row to be removed. This can leave orphaned child rows and requires controlled use. ON DELETE CASCADE on the child foreign key makes Oracle delete matching SALES rows automatically when the referenced STORES row is deleted.

questions.stem:

Evaluate the following query:

What would be the outcome?

SELECT INITCAP(cust_first_name || ' ' ||
               UPPER(SUBSTR(cust_city, -LENGTH(cust_city), 2)))
FROM customers
WHERE cust_first_name = 'Abigail';

options.text: Abigail Pa
options.explanation: LENGTH(Paris) is 5, so SUBSTR(Paris,-5,2) starts at the first character and returns Pa. UPPER changes it to PA, and the outer INITCAP changes the combined text to Abigail Pa.

options.explanation: Abigail PA is the intermediate value before INITCAP. INITCAP lowercases the remaining letters of each word after capitalizing the first letter.

options.text: An error message
options.explanation: LENGTH, SUBSTR, UPPER, concatenation, and INITCAP are valid in this expression, so the query does not fail.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true regarding constraints?

options.text: A foreign key column cannot contain null values.
options.explanation: A foreign-key column can contain NULL unless a separate NOT NULL constraint prohibits it. A NULL foreign key does not have to match a parent key value.

options.text: A column with the UNIQUE constraint can contain null values.
options.explanation: UNIQUE prevents duplicate non-null values. Oracle can store multiple NULL values because NULL is not treated as equal to another NULL for uniqueness enforcement.

options.text: A constraint is enforced only for an INSERT operation on the table.
options.explanation: Constraints can be checked during INSERT, UPDATE, and in referential cases DELETE. Enforcement is not limited to INSERT.

options.text: A constraint can be disabled even if the constraint column contains data.
options.explanation: A constraint can be disabled while the table contains data. Disabling controls future enforcement; ENABLE VALIDATE can later check existing rows.

options.text: All constraints can be defined at the column level and at the table level.
options.explanation: The reviewer selects this statement. In standard Oracle syntax, NOT NULL is defined only at column level, while many other constraints can be defined at column or table level.

questions.answerExplanation: UNIQUE prevents duplicate non-null values. Oracle can store multiple NULL values because NULL is not treated as equal to another NULL for uniqueness enforcement. The reviewer selects this statement. In standard Oracle syntax, NOT NULL is defined only at column level, while many other constraints can be defined at column or table level.
questions.technicalNote: The reviewer selects B and E. NOT NULL is the important exception to the claim in E because it is a column-level constraint. D describes a valid constraint-management operation. Scoring remains B and E.

questions.stem: Which two partitioned-table maintenance operations support asynchronous Global Index Maintenance in Oracle Database 12c?

options.text: ALTER TABLE SPLIT PARTITION
options.explanation: SPLIT PARTITION redistributes rows into new partitions and is not one of the operations selected for asynchronous global-index cleanup in this question.

options.text: ALTER TABLE MERGE PARTITION
options.explanation: MERGE PARTITION combines partitions and is not one of the two selected asynchronous-maintenance operations.

options.text: ALTER TABLE TRUNCATE PARTITION
options.explanation: TRUNCATE PARTITION removes all rows from a partition. With asynchronous global index maintenance, index cleanup can be deferred rather than performed fully in the foreground operation.

options.text: ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION
options.explanation: ADD PARTITION introduces an empty partition and does not remove indexed row entries that require asynchronous cleanup.

options.text: ALTER TABLE DROP PARTITION
options.explanation: DROP PARTITION removes a partition and its rows. Asynchronous global index maintenance can defer cleanup of affected global-index entries.

options.text: ALTER TABLE MOVE PARTITION
options.explanation: MOVE PARTITION relocates partition data and is not one of the two operations selected here.

questions.answerExplanation: TRUNCATE PARTITION removes all rows from a partition. With asynchronous global index maintenance, index cleanup can be deferred rather than performed fully in the foreground operation. DROP PARTITION removes a partition and its rows. Asynchronous global index maintenance can defer cleanup of affected global-index entries.

questions.stem: Examine the PRODUCTS and SALES tables. You issue the following query to display each product name and the number of times the product has been sold. What happens when the statement is executed?

FROM (

  FROM sales
  GROUP BY prod_id
) i RIGHT OUTER JOIN products p
  ON i.prod_id = p.prod_id;

options.text: The statement executes successfully and produces the required output.
options.explanation: An inline view can contain GROUP BY and participate in an outer join. The ITEM_CNT alias becomes available to the outer query.

options.text: The statement produces an error because a subquery in the FROM clause and outer joins cannot be used together.

options.explanation: An inline view may contain grouping and aggregate functions.

options.explanation: ITEM_CNT is an exposed column alias of inline view i and can be selected by the outer query.

questions.stem: Examine the following statement. On which two columns will an index be created automatically?

codeBlocks.title: Statement
codeBlocks.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  serial_no NUMBER UNIQUE,
  order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date DATE NOT NULL,
  status VARCHAR2(10) CHECK (status IN ('CREDIT', 'CASH')),
  product_id NUMBER REFERENCES products(product_id),
  order_total NUMBER
);

options.text: SERIAL_NO
options.explanation: Oracle normally creates or reuses a unique index to enforce the UNIQUE constraint.

options.text: PRODUCT_ID
options.explanation: Oracle does not automatically create an index for a foreign-key constraint on the child table.

options.text: ORDER_TOTAL
options.explanation: No primary-key or unique constraint is defined on this column.

options.text: ORDER_ID
options.explanation: Oracle normally creates or reuses a unique index to enforce the primary-key constraint.

options.text: STATUS
options.explanation: A CHECK constraint does not automatically create an index.

options.text: ORDER_DATE
options.explanation: A NOT NULL constraint does not automatically create an index.

questions.answerExplanation: Oracle normally creates or reuses a unique index to enforce the UNIQUE constraint. Oracle normally creates or reuses a unique index to enforce the primary-key constraint.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about the data dictionary?

options.explanation: Oracle maintains dictionary information as database objects, privileges, and related metadata change.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about date/time functions in a session where NLS_DATE_FORMAT is set to DD-MON-YYYY HH24:MI:SS?

questions.stem: You have been granted the CREATE ANY INDEX system privilege. You want to create an index on a table in another schema to which you have been granted only the SELECT privilege. Which two statements are true?

options.text: You additionally require the INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and INDEX privileges on the table.
options.explanation: These additional object privileges are not required when the necessary system privilege is already held.

options.text: You must have either the UNLIMITED TABLESPACE system privilege or sufficient quota on the tablespace where the index will be created.
options.explanation: The index is associated with the table owner’s schema, so the relevant storage authority belongs to the table owner.

options.text: The owner of the table must have either the UNLIMITED TABLESPACE system privilege or sufficient quota on the tablespace where the index will be created.
options.explanation: The table owner must have sufficient tablespace allocation for the index segment.

options.text: You additionally require only the INDEX privilege on the table.
options.explanation: The CREATE ANY INDEX system privilege provides the authorization to create an index on another schema’s table.

options.text: The owner of the table must also have the CREATE ANY INDEX system privilege.
options.explanation: The owner does not need this system privilege for another authorized user to create the index.

options.text: You do not require any further object privileges on the table.
options.explanation: The CREATE ANY INDEX system privilege is sufficient without additional object privileges on the table.

questions.answerExplanation: The table owner must have sufficient tablespace allocation for the index segment. The CREATE ANY INDEX system privilege is sufficient without additional object privileges on the table.

questions.stem: Examine the data in the COLORS and BRICKS tables. Which two queries return all the rows from COLORS?

options.text:
SELECT *
FROM bricks b
RIGHT JOIN colors c
ON b.color_rgb_hex_value = c.rgb_hex_value;
options.explanation: The right outer join preserves every row from COLORS, including colors without a matching brick.

options.text:
SELECT *
FROM colors c
LEFT JOIN bricks b
ON b.color_rgb_hex_value = c.rgb_hex_value
WHERE b.brick_id > 0;
options.explanation: The WHERE condition removes rows for colors without matching bricks because their BRICK_ID values are null.

options.text:
SELECT *
FROM bricks b
FULL JOIN colors c
ON b.color_rgb_hex_value = c.rgb_hex_value;
options.explanation: A full outer join preserves all rows from both tables, including every row from COLORS.

options.text:
SELECT *
FROM bricks b
JOIN colors c
ON b.color_rgb_hex_value = c.rgb_hex_value;
options.explanation: An inner join returns only colors with matching brick rows.

options.text:
SELECT *
FROM colors c
LEFT JOIN bricks b
USING (rgb_hex_value);
options.explanation: The displayed tables do not have a same-named RGB_HEX_VALUE column on both sides. The BRICKS column is COLOR_RGB_HEX_VALUE.

questions.answerExplanation: The right outer join preserves every row from COLORS, including colors without a matching brick. A full outer join preserves all rows from both tables, including every row from COLORS.
questions.technicalNote: The two data tables must render separately. RIGHT JOIN and FULL JOIN preserve all rows from COLORS; a filter on the nullable BRICKS side after a LEFT JOIN removes unmatched colors.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true about privileges?

options.text: Object privileges granted on a table automatically apply to all synonyms for that table.
options.explanation: A synonym is only an alternate name. When SQL resolves the synonym, access is still checked against the underlying table, so existing table privileges apply through the synonym.

options.text: All types of schema objects have associated object privileges.
options.explanation: Object privileges are defined only for object types that support grantable operations. Not every schema-object type has its own object privileges.

options.text: Only users with GRANT ANY PRIVILEGE can grant and revoke system privileges from other users.
options.explanation: The reviewer uses GRANT ANY PRIVILEGE as the authority for passing system privileges. A user who received a particular system privilege WITH ADMIN OPTION can also pass that specific privilege onward.

options.text: Only users with the DBA role can create roles.
options.explanation: CREATE ROLE is the required system privilege. Holding the DBA role is one possible source of authority but is not the only conceptual requirement.

options.text: Schema owners can grant object privileges on objects in their schema to any other user or role.
options.explanation: An object owner can grant applicable privileges on owned objects to users or roles, optionally with grant authority where supported.

options.text: A combination of object and system privileges can be granted to a role.
options.explanation: Roles can contain system privileges, object privileges, and other roles. The reviewer does not select this statement, so the broader role-composition rule is clarified in the technical note.

questions.answerExplanation: A synonym is only an alternate name. When SQL resolves the synonym, access is still checked against the underlying table, so existing table privileges apply through the synonym. The reviewer uses GRANT ANY PRIVILEGE as the authority for passing system privileges. A user who received a particular system privilege WITH ADMIN OPTION can also pass that specific privilege onward. An object owner can grant applicable privileges on owned objects to users or roles, optionally with grant authority where supported.
questions.technicalNote: The reviewer selects A, C, and E. A system privilege can also be passed by a grantee who received it WITH ADMIN OPTION, and roles can contain both system and object privileges. Scoring remains A, C, and E.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about the WITH GRANT OPTION clause?

options.text: The grantee must have the GRANT ANY OBJECT PRIVILEGE system privilege to use this option.
options.explanation: WITH GRANT OPTION itself authorizes the grantee to pass the received object privilege onward; GRANT ANY OBJECT PRIVILEGE is not additionally required for that privilege.

options.text: It can be used when granting privileges to roles.
options.explanation: Object privileges granted to a role cannot include WITH GRANT OPTION. The option is used when granting directly to a user or PUBLIC.

options.text: The grantee can grant the object privilege to any user in the database with this option.
options.explanation: A grantee with WITH GRANT OPTION can pass the object privilege to another user or PUBLIC, subject to the scope of the received privilege.

options.text: It can be used for system and object privileges.
options.explanation: The reviewer applies this wording to both privilege categories. Oracle terminology uses WITH GRANT OPTION for object privileges and WITH ADMIN OPTION for system privileges.

options.text: It can be used to pass on privileges to other users by the grantee.
options.explanation: WITH GRANT OPTION lets the recipient grant the same object privilege to other users or PUBLIC.

options.text: It cannot be used to pass on privileges to PUBLIC by the grantee.
options.explanation: The option can permit granting to PUBLIC, so saying it cannot be passed to PUBLIC is too restrictive.

questions.answerExplanation: The reviewer applies this wording to both privilege categories. Oracle terminology uses WITH GRANT OPTION for object privileges and WITH ADMIN OPTION for system privileges. WITH GRANT OPTION lets the recipient grant the same object privilege to other users or PUBLIC.
questions.technicalNote: The reviewer selects D and E. Oracle uses different clauses: WITH GRANT OPTION for object privileges and WITH ADMIN OPTION for system privileges. C also reflects the onward-grant capability provided to a user. Scoring remains D and E.

questions.stem: Which three actions can you perform only with system privileges?

options.text: Use the WITH GRANT OPTION clause.
options.explanation: WITH GRANT OPTION belongs to an object-privilege grant; it is not itself an action that can be performed only with a system privilege.

options.text: Log in to a database instance.
options.explanation: CREATE SESSION is the system privilege that permits a user to establish a database session.

options.text: Access flat files stored in an operating-system directory through UTL_FILE.
options.explanation: UTL_FILE access requires EXECUTE on the package and appropriate privileges on an Oracle DIRECTORY object. The reviewer classifies this under system-level or directory authorization.

options.text: Query any table in a database.
options.explanation: SELECT ANY TABLE is a system privilege that can authorize querying tables across schemas, although SELECT on a specific table can also be granted as an object privilege.

options.text: Execute a procedure in another schema.
options.explanation: A user can execute a specific procedure in another schema through the EXECUTE object privilege; a system-wide privilege is not always required.

questions.answerExplanation: WITH GRANT OPTION belongs to an object-privilege grant; it is not itself an action that can be performed only with a system privilege. CREATE SESSION is the system privilege that permits a user to establish a database session. UTL_FILE access requires EXECUTE on the package and appropriate privileges on an Oracle DIRECTORY object. The reviewer classifies this under system-level or directory authorization.
questions.technicalNote: The reviewer selects A, B, and C. WITH GRANT OPTION is associated with object privileges, and querying any table can be authorized by SELECT ANY TABLE. The distinction between system privileges and object privileges is the central clarification.

questions.stem: What is true about non-equijoin statement performance?

options.text: Table aliases can improve performance.
options.explanation: Aliases shorten table references and disambiguate columns, but the optimizer does not produce a faster plan merely because an alias is used.

options.text: The BETWEEN condition always performs better than using the >= and <= conditions.
options.explanation: BETWEEN is logically equivalent to >= lower_bound AND <= upper_bound for an inclusive range. Neither form is guaranteed always to outperform the other.

options.text: The join syntax used makes no difference to performance.
options.explanation: Logically equivalent Oracle and ANSI join syntax can be transformed into the same execution plan, so syntax alone often makes no performance difference.

options.text: The BETWEEN condition always performs less well than using the >= and <= conditions.
options.explanation: This statement uses the absolute word always. The optimizer generally treats BETWEEN and equivalent comparison predicates alike rather than guaranteeing worse performance.

options.text: The Oracle join syntax performs better than the SQL:1999-compliant ANSI join syntax.
options.explanation: Traditional Oracle join syntax is not inherently faster than ANSI join syntax. Performance depends on the execution plan, statistics, indexes, and data distribution.

questions.answerExplanation: This statement uses the absolute word always. The optimizer generally treats BETWEEN and equivalent comparison predicates alike rather than guaranteeing worse performance. Traditional Oracle join syntax is not inherently faster than ANSI join syntax. Performance depends on the execution plan, statistics, indexes, and data distribution.
questions.technicalNote: The reviewer selects D and E. Equivalent range predicates and logically equivalent join syntax normally do not guarantee a performance difference. C expresses the more typical optimizer behavior. Scoring remains D and E.

questions.stem: You must create a column for a banking application. Which data type meets all three requirements?

sections.title: Requirement 1
sections.content: Be stored in a format that supports date arithmetic without using conversion functions.

sections.title: Requirement 2
sections.content: Store a loan period of up to 10 years.

sections.title: Requirement 3
sections.content: Be used to calculate interest according to the number of days the loan remains unpaid.

options.text: INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH
options.explanation: This interval stores durations in years and months, not directly in days.

options.text: TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE
options.explanation: This stores a point in time with time-zone information rather than an elapsed duration.

options.text: INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND
options.explanation: This interval stores durations in days, hours, minutes, and seconds and supports date arithmetic.

options.text: TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE
options.explanation: This represents a date and time normalized according to time-zone rules, not a loan duration.

options.text: TIMESTAMP
options.explanation: A timestamp represents a point in time rather than an elapsed period.

questions.answerExplanation: This interval stores durations in days, hours, minutes, and seconds and supports date arithmetic.

questions.stem: Examine the EMPLOYEES table. Which two queries return rows for employees whose manager works in a different department?

options.text:
SELECT emp.*
FROM employees emp RIGHT JOIN employees mgr
ON emp.manager_id = mgr.employee_id
AND emp.department_id <> mgr.department_id
WHERE emp.employee_id IS NOT NULL;
options.explanation: The RIGHT JOIN preserves manager rows, while WHERE emp.employee_id IS NOT NULL removes unmatched manager-only results. The remaining rows are employees whose matched manager has a different department, making this structurally similar to an inner join.

options.text:
SELECT emp.*
FROM employees emp LEFT JOIN employees mgr
ON emp.manager_id = mgr.employee_id
AND emp.department_id <> mgr.department_id;
options.explanation: The LEFT JOIN preserves every employee even when no manager row satisfies the different-department condition. Unmatched employees therefore appear with null manager columns, which broadens the result beyond the stated requirement.

options.text:
SELECT emp.*
FROM employees emp JOIN employees mgr
ON emp.manager_id = mgr.employee_id
AND emp.department_id <> mgr.department_id;
options.explanation: The inner self-join matches each employee to the row identified by MANAGER_ID and keeps only pairs with different DEPARTMENT_ID values.

options.text:
SELECT emp.*
FROM employees emp
WHERE manager_id NOT IN (
SELECT mgr.employee_id
FROM employees mgr
WHERE emp.department_id <> mgr.department_id
);
options.explanation: NOT IN asks whether MANAGER_ID is absent from a broad set of employee IDs and does not correlate the employee to the employee’s actual manager department correctly.

options.text:
SELECT emp.*
FROM employees emp
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
SELECT NULL
FROM employees mgr
WHERE emp.manager_id = mgr.employee_id
AND emp.department_id <> mgr.department_id
);
options.explanation: NOT EXISTS returns employees for whom no different-department manager match exists, the opposite of the requested condition.

questions.answerExplanation: The LEFT JOIN preserves every employee even when no manager row satisfies the different-department condition. Unmatched employees therefore appear with null manager columns, which broadens the result beyond the stated requirement. The inner self-join matches each employee to the row identified by MANAGER_ID and keeps only pairs with different DEPARTMENT_ID values.
questions.technicalNote: The reviewer selects B and C. Because B is a LEFT JOIN without a filter on the manager side, it also preserves employees lacking a qualifying different-department match. A and C more directly restrict the result to matched employee-manager pairs. Scoring remains B and C.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about savepoints?

options.text: After issuing a savepoint, you can roll back to the savepoint name within the current transaction.
options.explanation: ROLLBACK TO savepoint_name reverses changes made after that savepoint and keeps the transaction active. Earlier uncommitted changes remain pending.

options.text: A ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT command issued before the start of a transaction results in an error.
options.explanation: ROLLBACK TO requires an existing savepoint in the current transaction. If the savepoint does not exist, Oracle raises a savepoint-related error.

options.text: Savepoints make uncommitted updates visible to other sessions owned by the same user.
options.explanation: Uncommitted data is visible only within the session that made the changes, even when another session uses the same database account.

options.text: After issuing a savepoint, you cannot roll back the complete transaction.
options.explanation: A plain ROLLBACK can still reverse the complete transaction after savepoints have been created.

options.text: You can commit updates performed between two savepoints without committing other updates in the current transaction.
options.explanation: The reviewer selects this statement, but Oracle COMMIT applies to the entire current transaction. Savepoints cannot divide one transaction into independently committable portions.

options.text: Savepoints make uncommitted updates visible to sessions owned by other users.
options.explanation: Savepoints do not alter transaction isolation or expose uncommitted rows to other users.

questions.answerExplanation: ROLLBACK TO savepoint_name reverses changes made after that savepoint and keeps the transaction active. Earlier uncommitted changes remain pending. The reviewer selects this statement, but Oracle COMMIT applies to the entire current transaction. Savepoints cannot divide one transaction into independently committable portions.
questions.technicalNote: The reviewer selects A and E. Oracle cannot commit only the work between savepoints; COMMIT ends and commits the whole transaction. B also describes the behavior when the named savepoint does not exist. Scoring remains A and E.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true about performing Data Manipulation Language operations on a view with no INSTEAD OF triggers defined?

options.text: DELETE statements can always be performed on a table through a view.
options.explanation: DELETE through a view depends on whether the view is inherently updatable and whether the affected underlying table can be identified. It is not guaranteed for every view.

options.text: Views cannot be used to query rows from an underlying table if the table has a primary key and the primary-key columns are not referenced in the view’s defining query.
options.explanation: A view can query selected columns without including a primary key. Primary-key columns are not required merely to read rows through the view.

options.text: Views cannot be used to add rows to an underlying table if the table has NOT NULL columns without default values that are not referenced in the view’s defining query.
options.explanation: An INSERT through the view cannot provide values for omitted NOT NULL columns that have no defaults, so the underlying insert cannot succeed.

options.text: INSERT statements can always be performed on a table through a view.
options.explanation: INSERT through a view depends on view updatability and whether required underlying columns can receive values. It is not guaranteed for every view.

options.text: Views cannot be used to add or modify rows in an underlying table if the defining query contains the DISTINCT keyword.
options.explanation: DISTINCT makes the view non-key-preserved for DML purposes; rows cannot be added or modified through that view without an appropriate INSTEAD OF trigger.

options.text: The WITH CHECK clause has no effect when deleting rows from the underlying table through the view.
options.explanation: WITH CHECK OPTION constrains inserts and updates so rows remain visible through the view condition. It does not control DELETE in the same way.

questions.answerExplanation: DELETE through a view depends on whether the view is inherently updatable and whether the affected underlying table can be identified. It is not guaranteed for every view. An INSERT through the view cannot provide values for omitted NOT NULL columns that have no defaults, so the underlying insert cannot succeed. INSERT through a view depends on view updatability and whether required underlying columns can receive values. It is not guaranteed for every view.
questions.technicalNote: The reviewer selects A, C, and D. A and D use the word always, while view DML actually depends on inherent updatability. E also states an important restriction for DISTINCT views. Scoring remains A, C, and D.

questions.stem: Examine the EMPLOYEES table. Which three queries return all rows whose SALARY plus COMMISSION is greater than 20000?

options.text:
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE NVL(salary + commission, 0) >= 20000;
options.explanation: If COMMISSION is null, SALARY + COMMISSION becomes null before NVL is applied, resulting in zero.

options.text:
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE salary + NVL2(commission, commission, 0) >= 20000;
options.explanation: NVL2 returns the commission when non-null and zero when null, allowing the total to be calculated.

options.text:
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE salary + NULLIF(commission, 0) >= 20000;
options.explanation: NULLIF returns null when commission is zero and also leaves null commissions null, which can make the total null.

options.text:
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE NVL2(salary + NULLIF(commission, 0), salary + commission, salary) >= 20000;
options.explanation: The expression returns the calculated total when available and otherwise returns the salary.

options.text:
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE salary + NVL(commission, 0) >= 20000;
options.explanation: NVL converts a null commission to zero before adding it to the salary.

options.text:
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE CEIL(salary, commission) >= 20000;
options.explanation: CEIL accepts one numeric argument and does not add salary and commission.

questions.answerExplanation: NVL2 returns the commission when non-null and zero when null, allowing the total to be calculated. The expression returns the calculated total when available and otherwise returns the salary. NVL converts a null commission to zero before adding it to the salary.

questions.stem: BOOK_SEQ is an existing sequence in your schema. Which two CREATE TABLE commands are valid?

options.explanation: CURRVAL depends on NEXTVAL having already been referenced in the session and is not the sequence expression used for an automatic new key default. A default intended to generate keys uses NEXTVAL.
BOOK_SEQ.CURRVAL is written as if it were a standalone column definition, which is invalid. END_DATE also attempts to reference START_DATE in a column default, which is not allowed this way.
All columns have valid data types and constraints. BK_ID is a not-null primary key, START_DATE is required, and END_DATE receives SYSDATE when omitted.
BOOK_SEQ.NEXTVAL is a valid sequence-based default for BK_ID in the targeted Oracle version. The primary key, date defaults, and NOT NULL constraint are syntactically consistent.
START_DATE has no declared data type, and END_DATE tries to calculate a default from other row columns. Both prevent the CREATE TABLE statement from succeeding.

questions.answerExplanation: All columns have valid data types and constraints. BK_ID is a not-null primary key, START_DATE is required, and END_DATE receives SYSDATE when omitted. BOOK_SEQ.NEXTVAL is a valid sequence-based default for BK_ID in the targeted Oracle version. The primary key, date defaults, and NOT NULL constraint are syntactically consistent.
questions.technicalNote: Sequence NEXTVAL in a column default is version-dependent in older Oracle releases but is valid in the reviewer’s target context. CURRVAL is session-dependent and is not appropriate for generating the next booking key.

questions.stem: You execute the following SQL statement. Which three statements are true?

codeBlocks.title: SQL statement
codeBlocks.code:
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (
23, 2300, SYSDATE,
(SELECT channel_id
FROM channels
WHERE channels_desc = 'Direct Sales'),
12, 1, 500
);

options.text: The statement executes successfully, and a new row is inserted into the SALES table.
options.explanation: The scalar subquery supplies one CHANNEL_ID value for Direct Sales. If it returns exactly one row and all constraints are satisfied, the INSERT supplies a complete SALES row and succeeds.

options.text: A product can have a different unit price at different times.
options.explanation: The inserted row includes its own unit-price value. Because price is stored with the sales fact rather than only in PRODUCTS, the same product can be recorded at different prices at different times.

options.text: The statement fails because a subquery may not be contained in a VALUES clause.
options.explanation: A scalar subquery can be used as an expression in a VALUES list when it returns at most one row and one column.

options.text: The statement fails if a row already exists in the SALES table for product 23.
options.explanation: A product can appear in multiple sales rows. PROD_ID is a foreign key, not a unique key on SALES, so an existing row for product 23 does not by itself block another sale.

options.text: A customer can exist in many countries.
options.explanation: The shown model associates each customer with a country through the customer data. It does not show one customer belonging simultaneously to many countries.

options.text: The SALES table has five foreign keys.
options.explanation: The schema relationships show SALES referencing five dimensions or parent tables: PRODUCTS, CUSTOMERS, TIMES, CHANNELS, and PROMOTIONS.

questions.answerExplanation: The scalar subquery supplies one CHANNEL_ID value for Direct Sales. If it returns exactly one row and all constraints are satisfied, the INSERT supplies a complete SALES row and succeeds. The inserted row includes its own unit-price value. Because price is stored with the sales fact rather than only in PRODUCTS, the same product can be recorded at different prices at different times. The schema relationships show SALES referencing five dimensions or parent tables: PRODUCTS, CUSTOMERS, TIMES, CHANNELS, and PROMOTIONS.
questions.technicalNote: The schema diagram is intentionally omitted from the JSON because the supplied image is blurred and contains many tables. The explanations preserve only the relationships needed for the highlighted answers. The INSERT still depends on the scalar subquery returning one CHANNEL_ID and on all constraints being satisfied.
